attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Aren't going away, anytime soon' is firm, unhedged language, so it is a scored forecast. The proposition keeps both the claim that hallucinations persist now and the near-term horizon.

contract.note: The speaker gave no date, so the one-year window is the evaluator's reading. It is an ordinary reading of 'anytime soon'. Saying that lower rates do not count as 'going away' is also fair. A longer window would only make support stronger.

evidence.note: Sept 2025 preprint by OpenAI researchers, inside the window, saying hallucinations persist even in state-of-the-art systems.
Independent preprint from May 2026, inside the window. It measures 4.6–6.1% package-hallucination rates in frontier models released up to March 2026. Later revisions kept the headline rates.
OpenAI's own system card reports reduced hallucinations, not eliminated ones. This is a company disclosure and does not meet the contradiction condition.
Court-case count dated to the evaluation date, after the window. It shows hallucinated filings continued, but it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The one-year window has passed. Evidence from inside the window (e1, e2) shows frontier models still hallucinating at material rates, and researchers describe the problem as persisting. The counterevidence (e3) shows reduction, not elimination. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: This describes the state of things at the time of the post. 'Seem' describes how lawyers appear; it is not a probability hedge. The scope words 'a lot' and 'many' are kept.

contract.note: No thresholds are stated. The contract reads 'a lot' as substantial survey use and 'seem shocked' as continued fabricated filings by lawyers who appear unaware of the risk. Both are ordinary, fair readings.

evidence.note: Survey of nearly 400 lawyers fielded through Jan 2025: 40% use generative AI for research and over a quarter for document creation. It covers generative AI in general, not ChatGPT specifically, which still fits 'tools like ChatGPT'.
LA Times report from May 2025: about 30 lawyer cases with AI-generated errors in 2025 alone, inside the target period.
The same LA Times column describes the lawyers as apparently oblivious, which matches the plain reading of 'seem shocked'.

reviews.rationale: Survey data from early 2025 shows substantial lawyer use of generative AI for research and drafting. Contemporary reporting shows a continuing stream of lawyer filings with fabricated citations in 2025, and the lawyers are described as unaware of the risk. The support condition is met, and no counterevidence was found.
